reference.source: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours (Odontogenic and Maxillofacial Bone Tumours) / Burket's Oral Medicine
clinicalPearls: A developmental odontogenic cyst arising from dental lamina remnants, with a notable tendency to recur
Most often found in the posterior mandible and ascending ramus
Grows along the marrow spaces in an anteroposterior direction with relatively little bony expansion, so it can become large before detection
Radiographs show a well-defined uni- or multilocular radiolucency, sometimes associated with an unerupted tooth

Histology is characteristic: a thin, uniform parakeratinised stratified squamous epithelium with a palisaded, hyperchromatic basal layer and a corrugated luminal surface, with friable keratin filling the lumen
The high recurrence rate is attributed to the thin friable lining and to satellite (daughter) cysts within the wall
Multiple keratocysts should prompt evaluation for the naevoid basal cell carcinoma (Gorlin-Goltz) syndrome, associated with PTCH1 mutations

Management options include enucleation with adjunctive measures such as peripheral ostectomy or chemical cauterisation, or decompression and marsupialisation, with resection reserved for aggressive or recurrent disease
reference.pathophysiology: The odontogenic keratocyst develops from remnants of the dental lamina and is lined by a distinctive keratinising epithelium whose basal cells show intrinsic proliferative activity, giving it a more neoplastic-like behaviour than ordinary odontogenic cysts. Growth occurs by mural expansion and extension through cancellous bone rather than by hydrostatic pressure alone, and small satellite cysts and epithelial islands within the fibrous capsule act as sources of recurrence if left behind. Inactivation of the PTCH1 tumour-suppressor gene in the sonic hedgehog pathway underlies both sporadic lesions and the multiple keratocysts of the naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome.
additionalInvestigations: Panoramic and cross-sectional imaging (CT/CBCT) to define extent and the relationship to teeth and canal
Incisional or aspiration biopsy, with aspirate typically showing low soluble protein and keratin
Histopathological examination for the characteristic parakeratinised lining
Evaluation for naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome when lesions are multiple or the patient is young, including skin, skeletal, and intracranial features
PTCH1 genetic testing and family assessment where the syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Multiple keratocysts or a young patient, prompting a search for Gorlin-Goltz syndrome
Syndromic features such as multiple basal cell carcinomas, palmar and plantar pits, and a calcified falx cerebri
Rapid growth, pain, or paraesthesia suggesting infection or aggressive behaviour
reference.prognosis: Individual cysts are benign and treatable, but recurrence is common, particularly after simple enucleation, so prolonged follow-up is essential; the prognosis is influenced by the treatment method and, in syndromic patients, by the tendency to form new cysts over time.
pitfalls: Treating with simple enucleation without adjunctive measures and incurring recurrence
Failing to recognise multiple cysts as a marker of Gorlin-Goltz syndrome
Confusing it with a dentigerous cyst and under-treating
references: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours (Odontogenic and Maxillofacial Bone Tumours)
management: Complete surgical removal is the mainstay, most often enucleation with curettage aimed at eliminating the friable lining and satellite cysts
Adjunctive treatment of the bony cavity after enucleation with Carnoy's solution or cryotherapy to destroy residual epithelium and reduce recurrence
Marsupialisation or decompression to shrink large lesions before definitive enucleation, lowering operative morbidity
En bloc or marginal resection reserved for large, aggressive or repeatedly recurrent lesions
Pre-operative panoramic and cross-sectional (CT/CBCT) imaging to define extent and relationship to teeth, canal and sinus
Prolonged radiographic surveillance for recurrence, which is common particularly after simple enucleation
Evaluation for naevoid basal cell carcinoma (Gorlin) syndrome when cysts are multiple or the patient is young, screening skin, skeletal and intracranial features
PTCH1 genetic testing, genetic counselling and family assessment where the syndrome is suspected
